SeeRevelation 1:20; Joseph Smith Translation, Revelation 1:20 (inRevelation 1:20, footnoteb).

SeeRevelation 1:4, 11;2;3. Historians believe John lived in Ephesus around the end of the first century and probably knew these Saints well before he was sent away to Patmos. It is not clear why these specific churches were singled out, as there were other branches of the Church established in Asia. Seven may have simply been symbolic, representing the entire Christian Church (see Draper and Rhodes,The Revelation of John the Apostle, 58; see also Alonzo L. Gaskill,The Lost Language of Symbolism: An Essential Guide for Recognizing and Interpreting Symbols of the Gospel[2003], 123–29).
See Richard D. Draper, “Understanding Images and Symbols in the Book of Revelation,” inShedding Light on the New Testament: Acts–Revelation, ed. Ray L. Huntington and others, (2009), 271–89.

See Matthew B. Brown and Paul T. Smith,Symbols in Stone: Symbolism on the Early Temples of the Restoration(1997), 102–3. The morning star is symbolized on early Latter-day Saint temples in the form of an inverted pentagram (five-pointed star). This symbolized the Restored Church of Jesus Christ, announcing the coming of the Son of God (see also Erastus Snow, inJournal of Discourses, 20:185).

Jeffrey R. Holland, in Face to Face with Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, Sister Carole M. Stephens, and Elder Donald L. Hallstrom (worldwide young adult broadcast, Mar. 8, 2016), 1:43:35–1:44:36, Gospel Library.

The Savior’s ultimate worthiness to fulfill the Father’s plan comes from His submission to the Father’s will and His atoning sacrifice for us (see Nicholas J. Frederick, “The Paradoxical Lamb and the Christology of John’s Apocalypse,” inThou Art the Christ, the Son of the Living God: The Person and Work of Jesus in the New Testament, ed. Eric D. Huntsman and others [2018], 262–63). Through that submission, He became mighty to save.

Scholars believe that the book of Revelation was written either around AD 60 during the reign of the emperor Nero or around AD 90 during the reign of emperor Domitian (see Eric D. Huntsman, “John, the Disciple Whom Jesus Loved,”Liahona, Jan. 2019, 22; see also Michael D. Coogan and others, eds.,The New Oxford Annotated Bible: New Revised Standard Version, 5th ed. [2018], 1805).

SeeIsaiah 11:1–10;Romans 15:12;Doctrine and Covenants 113:1–6. Although roots normally grow underground, this word can also refer to a branch, the part of the plant that grows up from the root (see Draper and Rhodes,The Revelation of John the Apostle, 229).
